title: IV. The Second Ordeal
paragraphs: “You can’t imagine how much you encourage us, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, by being so willing to answer,” said Nikolay Parfenovitch. He looked animated, and obvious satisfaction shone in his very prominent, short-sighted, light gray eyes, from which he had just taken off his spectacles. “And you made a very fair point about mutual trust. In cases this important, we sometimes simply can’t get anywhere without it, as long as the suspect truly hopes to defend himself and is able to. For our part, we will do everything we can, and you can see for yourself how we are handling the case. Do you agree, Ippolit Kirillovitch?” He turned to the prosecutor.
“Oh, certainly,” replied the prosecutor. Next to Nikolay Parfenovitch’s eagerness, he sounded rather cold.

Let me say right now, once and for all, that Nikolay Parfenovitch had only recently come to our town. From the start he had felt a marked respect for Ippolit Kirillovitch, our prosecutor, and had become almost his bosom friend. He was nearly the only person who trusted without reservation in Ippolit Kirillovitch’s extraordinary gifts as a psychologist and an orator, and in the justice of his grievance. He had heard of him back in Petersburg. In return, young Nikolay Parfenovitch was the only person in the world whom our “unappreciated” prosecutor really liked. On the road to Mokroe they had found time to agree on how to handle this case. Now, sitting at the table, the sharp-witted junior read every sign on his senior colleague’s face—half a word, a glance, a wink—and understood it at once.
“Gentlemen, just let me tell it my own way and don’t break in with petty questions, and I’ll tell you everything in a minute,” said Mitya excitedly.

“Excellent! Thank you. But before we listen to your account, may I ask about one more small matter that interests us a great deal? I mean the ten roubles you borrowed yesterday around five o’clock from your friend Pyotr Ilyitch Perhotin, with your pistols as security.”
“I pawned them, gentlemen. I pawned them for ten roubles. What else is there to say? That’s all of it. The moment I got back to town, I pawned them.”
“You got back to town? So you had been out of town?”
“Yes, I took a trip of forty versts out into the country. Didn’t you know?”
The prosecutor and Nikolay Parfenovitch looked at each other.

“Well, why don’t you start your story with a proper step-by-step account of everything you did yesterday, from morning on? Let us ask, for instance, why you were away from town, exactly when you left and when you came back—all those facts.”

“You should have asked me that way from the start,” cried Mitya, laughing out loud. “And if you like, we won’t begin with yesterday but with the morning of the day before. Then you’ll see how, why and where I went. The day before yesterday, gentlemen, I went to a merchant here in town, a man called Samsonov, to borrow three thousand roubles from him on safe security. It was urgent, gentlemen. I suddenly needed the money badly.”
“Excuse me for interrupting,” the prosecutor put in politely. “Why did you need exactly that sum, three thousand, so urgently?”

“Oh, gentlemen, there’s no need to go into the details, how, when and why, and why exactly this much money and not that much, and all that rigmarole. Why, it would fill three volumes, and then you’d want an epilogue!”
Mitya said all this with the good-natured but impatient familiarity of a man who is eager to tell the whole truth and means well.

“Gentlemen!”—he corrected himself hurriedly—“don’t be cross with me for being so restless, I’m asking you again. Believe me, I have the greatest respect for you, and I understand how matters really stand. Don’t think I’m drunk. I’m perfectly sober now. And being drunk wouldn’t get in my way anyhow. With me, you know, it’s just like the saying: ‘When he is sober, he is a fool; when he is drunk, he is a wise man.’ Ha ha! But I can see, gentlemen, that it isn’t right to joke with you, not until we’ve had our explanation, that is. And I have my own dignity to keep up, too. I understand the difference for now, believe me. After all, I’m in the position of a criminal, so I’m far from your equal. And it’s your job to keep an eye on me. I can’t expect you to pat me on the head for what I did to Grigory, because nobody breaks an old man’s head and gets off free. I suppose you’ll lock me up for him for six months, or maybe a year, in a house of correction. I don’t know what the punishment is—but it will be without loss of the rights of my rank, without loss of my rank, won’t it? So you see, gentlemen, I understand the distinction between us.... But surely you see that questions like these would baffle God Himself. ‘How did you step? Where did you step? When did you step? And on what did you step?’ I’ll get all muddled if you go on like this, and you’ll write it all down against me. And where will that get us? Nowhere! And even if I’m talking nonsense now, let me finish, and you, gentlemen, being men of honor and refinement, will forgive me! I’ll finish by asking you, gentlemen, to drop that conventional way of questioning. I mean this: you start with some miserable trifle, how I got up, what I had for breakfast, how I spat and where I spat, and so you lull the criminal’s attention, and then you suddenly knock him flat with an overwhelming question: ‘Whom did you murder? Whom did you rob?’ Ha ha! That’s your regular method, that’s where all your cunning comes in. You can catch peasants off guard that way, but not me. I know the tricks. I’ve been in the service, too. Ha ha ha! You’re not angry, gentlemen? You forgive my impertinence?” he cried, looking at them with a good nature that was almost startling. “It’s only Mitya Karamazov, you know, so you can let it pass. In a sensible man it would be inexcusable, but in Mitya you can forgive it. Ha ha!”

Nikolay Parfenovitch listened, and laughed along. The prosecutor didn’t laugh. He kept his eyes fixed sharply on Mitya, as if afraid of missing a single syllable, the slightest movement, the least twitch in any feature of his face.

“That’s how we’ve treated you from the very beginning,” said Nikolay Parfenovitch, still laughing. “We haven’t tried to throw you off by asking how you got out of bed in the morning or what you had for breakfast. In fact, we started with questions of the greatest importance.”

“I understand. I saw it, and I appreciated it. I appreciate even more the kindness you are showing me now, a kindness unheard of, and worthy of your noble hearts. The three of us here are gentlemen, so let everything stand on mutual trust between educated, well-bred men, joined by the common bond of noble birth and honor. In any case, let me regard you as my best friends at this moment of my life, when my honor is under attack. That’s no insult to you, gentlemen, is it?”
“On the contrary. You have put all that so well, Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” Nikolay Parfenovitch answered, with dignified approval.
“And enough of those petty questions, gentlemen, all those tricky questions!” cried Mitya enthusiastically. “Or there’s no telling where we’ll end up! Is there?”

“I will follow your sensible advice entirely,” the prosecutor interposed, addressing Mitya. “But I am not withdrawing my question. It is vitally important for us now to know exactly why you needed that sum, I mean precisely three thousand.”
“Why I needed it?... Oh, for one reason and another.... Well, it was to pay a debt.”
“A debt to whom?”

“That I flatly refuse to answer, gentlemen. Not because I can’t, or don’t dare, or because it would hurt me, since it’s all a paltry business and completely trivial, but—I won’t, because it’s a matter of principle: that’s my private life, and I won’t let anyone intrude on my private life. That’s my principle. Your question has nothing to do with the case, and whatever has nothing to do with the case is my own affair. I wanted to pay a debt. I wanted to pay a debt of honor, but to whom, I won’t say.”
“Let me make a note of that,” said the prosecutor.
“Go right ahead. Write down that I won’t say, that I won’t. Write that I’d think it dishonorable to say. Ech! Write it; you’ve got nothing else to do with your time.”

“Let me caution you, sir, and remind you once more, in case you don’t know,” the prosecutor began, with a peculiar and stern gravity, “that you have every right not to answer the questions put to you now. We, for our part, have no right to wring an answer out of you if you refuse to give one, for whatever reason. That is entirely up to you. But in cases like this one, it is our duty to explain to you and lay before you how much harm you will do yourself by refusing to give this or that piece of evidence. After that, I will ask you to continue.”
“Gentlemen, I’m not angry ... I ...” Mitya muttered, rather thrown off balance. “Well, gentlemen, you see, that Samsonov I went to then ...”

We will not, of course, repeat his account of what the reader already knows. Mitya was anxious, almost impatiently so, not to leave out the smallest detail. At the same time he was in a hurry to be done. But his evidence was being written down as he gave it, so they had to keep stopping him. Mitya disliked that, but he put up with it. He got angry, though still good-humoredly. From time to time, it is true, he cried out, “Gentlemen, that’s enough to wear out an angel’s patience!” Or, “Gentlemen, it’s no use getting me worked up.”

But even though he cried out, for a while he kept his genial, expansive mood. So he told them how Samsonov had made a fool of him two days earlier. (By now he fully understood that he had been fooled.) That he had sold his watch for six roubles to get money for the trip was news to the lawyers. They at once took a lively interest, and even thought it necessary, to Mitya’s intense indignation, to write the fact down as further proof that he had hardly a farthing in his pocket at the time. Little by little Mitya began to turn surly. Then he described his journey to see Lyagavy, the night in the stifling hut, and so on, and came to his return to town. Here, without much urging, he began to give a detailed account of the agonies of jealousy he had gone through over Grushenka.

They heard him in silent attention. They asked in particular about the lookout he had in Marya Kondratyevna’s house, at the back of Fyodor Pavlovitch’s garden, from which he watched for Grushenka, and about Smerdyakov bringing him news. They put special weight on this and noted it down. He spoke of his jealousy warmly and at length. Inwardly he was ashamed to expose his most intimate feelings to “public ignominy,” so to speak, but he plainly overcame his shame in order to tell the truth. The cold severity with which the investigating lawyer, and even more the prosecutor, stared at him as he talked finally threw him off quite badly.

“That boy, Nikolay Parfenovitch, to whom I was talking nonsense about women only a few days ago, and that sickly prosecutor are not worth my telling this to,” he reflected mournfully. “It’s ignominious. ‘Be patient, humble, hold thy peace.’” He closed his reflections with that line. But he pulled himself together and went on. When he got to his visit to Madame Hohlakov, his spirits came back, and he even wanted to tell a little anecdote about that lady that had nothing to do with the case. The investigating lawyer cut him off, however, and politely suggested he move on to “more essential matters.” Finally he described his despair, and told how, when he left Madame Hohlakov’s, he had thought he’d “get three thousand if he had to murder someone for it.” Again they stopped him, and noted down that he had “meant to murder someone.” Mitya let them write it without protest. At last he reached the point where he learned that Grushenka had deceived him: she had come back from Samsonov’s as soon as he left her there, though she had said she would stay until midnight.

“If I didn’t kill Fenya then, gentlemen, it was only because I had no time,” burst from him suddenly at that point. That, too, was carefully written down. Mitya waited gloomily and was starting to tell how he ran into his father’s garden, when the investigating lawyer suddenly stopped him. He opened the big portfolio lying on the sofa beside him and pulled out the brass pestle.
“Do you recognize this?” he asked, showing it to Mitya.
“Oh, yes,” Mitya laughed gloomily. “Of course I recognize it. Let me take a look at it.... Oh, damn it, never mind!”
“You forgot to mention it,” observed the investigating lawyer.
“Hang it all, I wasn’t hiding it from you. Do you think I could have got by without it? It just slipped my mind.”
“Please tell us exactly how you came to arm yourself with it.”
“Certainly, gentlemen, I’ll gladly tell you.”
And Mitya described how he picked up the pestle and ran.
“But what did you intend by arming yourself with such a weapon?”
“Intend? Nothing. I just grabbed it and ran off.”
“Why, if you had no intention?”

Mitya’s anger flared. He stared hard at “the boy” and smiled, gloomily and spitefully. He was feeling more and more ashamed that he had told “such people” the story of his jealousy so sincerely and so openly.
“Forget the pestle!” burst from him suddenly.
“But still—”
“Oh, to keep off dogs.... Oh, because it was dark.... In case something happened.”
“But did you ever before take a weapon along when you went out, if you’re so afraid of the dark?”
“Ugh! Damn it all, gentlemen! There’s simply no talking to you!” cried Mitya, driven past all endurance. He turned to the secretary, crimson with rage, and said quickly, his voice shaking with fury:

“Write this down at once ... at once ... ‘that I snatched up the pestle to go and kill my father ... Fyodor Pavlovitch ... by hitting him on the head with it!’ Well, are you satisfied now, gentlemen? Do you feel better?” he said, glaring defiantly at the lawyers.

“We understand perfectly that you made that statement just now out of exasperation with us and with our questions, which you think trivial, though in fact they are essential,” the prosecutor remarked dryly in reply.

“Well, honestly, gentlemen! Yes, I took the pestle.... What does a man pick things up for at such moments? I don’t know what for. I snatched it up and ran—that’s all. Because for me, gentlemen, _passons_, or I swear I won’t tell you any more.”

He sat with his elbows on the table and his head in his hand, turned sideways to them, staring at the wall and fighting down a feeling of nausea. He truly had an awful urge to stand up and announce that he wouldn’t say another word, “not if you hang me for it.”

“You see, gentlemen,” he said at last, controlling himself with difficulty, “you see. I listen to you and I’m haunted by a dream.... It’s a dream I have sometimes, you know.... I often have it—it’s always the same ... that someone is hunting me, someone I’m terribly afraid of ... that he’s hunting me in the dark, at night ... tracking me, and I hide from him somewhere, behind a door or a cupboard, hide in a degrading way, and the worst of it is that he always knows where I am, but he pretends not to know on purpose, to draw out my agony, to enjoy my terror.... That’s exactly what you’re doing now. It’s just like that!”
“Is that the kind of thing you dream about?” asked the prosecutor.
“Yes, it is. Don’t you want to write it down?” said Mitya, with a twisted smile.
“No, there’s no need to write it down. But you do have strange dreams.”
“It’s not about dreams now, gentlemen—this is realism, this is real life! I’m a wolf and you’re the hunters. Well, go on, hunt him down!”
“You are wrong to make such comparisons ...” began Nikolay Parfenovitch, with extraordinary gentleness.

“No, I’m not wrong, not at all!” Mitya flared up again, though his burst of anger had plainly eased his heart. He grew more good-humored with every word. “You may not trust a criminal, or a man on trial tortured by your questions, but an honorable man, the honorable impulses of the heart (I say that boldly!)—no! That you must believe, you have no right indeed ... but—
Be silent, heart, Be patient, humble, hold thy peace.
Well, shall I go on?” he broke off gloomily.
“If you’d be so kind,” answered Nikolay Parfenovitch.
